Bin points into hexagons or squares

Source: R/bins.R
sdv_bins.Rd

sdv_bins() bins x/y points into pointy-top hexagons (shape = "hex", the default) or axis-aligned squares (shape = "square") and returns one row per cell: its id, center, count and the rows it holds. sdv_bin_ids() returns each point's cell id instead, the key that links a point to its cell in an interactive chart (geom_sdv_bins_interactive()). The lattice is the one sdvplot (Python) and sdvplot-js (binner()) use, with the same argument names, so all three put the same points in the same cells with the same ids.

Usage

sdv_bins(
  x,
  y,
  shape = "hex",
  radius = NULL,
  side = NULL,
  equal_area = FALSE,
  origin = c(0, 0),
  weights = NULL
)

sdv_bin_ids(
  x,
  y,
  shape = "hex",
  radius = NULL,
  side = NULL,
  equal_area = FALSE,
  origin = c(0, 0)
)

Arguments

x, y

Numeric vectors of point coordinates, the same length.

shape

"hex" (the default) or "square".

radius

The hexagons' circumradius; for squares, with equal_area = TRUE, the circumradius of the hexagon whose area each square has.

side

The squares' side.

equal_area

For squares: size them by radius to the area of a hexagon of that circumradius, so a hex chart and a square chart of the same data have cells of the same area.

origin

The point a cell is centered on, c(x, y) in the points' units: a hoop-centered lattice, origin = the basket's coordinates. The default c(0, 0) centers a cell on the data origin.

weights

NULL (the default) or a numeric vector as long as x, each point's weight (points scored, say). A cell's weight is the sum of its points' weights; a missing or non-finite weight counts 0, but the point is still binned and counted.

Value

sdv_bins(): a data frame with one row per cell, in first-seen order:

col_nametypedescription
cell_idcharacterThe cell's id, "x,y" (see Details)
xnumericThe cell center's x, in the points' units
ynumericThe cell center's y, in the points' units
countintegerPoints in the cell
weightnumericThe sum of the cell's points' weights (its count without weights)
rowslistInteger positions (1-based) of the cell's points in x / y, in input order

sdv_bin_ids(): a character vector as long as x, each point's cell id (NA for a skipped point).

Details

Sizes are in the points' own units (data space, not pixels): a hexagon has circumradius radius, a square side side, and with equal_area = TRUE a square has the area of a hexagon of circumradius radius (side radius * sqrt(3 * sqrt(3) / 2), about 1.6119 * radius). Both lattices have a cell centered on origin, c(0, 0) by default: for a hoop-centered lattice, origin = the basket's coordinates (the points are binned as x - origin[1], y - origin[2] and the centers shifted back, so ids are still the absolute centers).

  • Hexagons are d3-hexbin's lattice: rows 1.5 * radius apart, columns sqrt(3) * radius apart, odd rows shifted half a column. Each point goes to the center d3-hexbin picks, which is close to but not exactly the nearest one, so about 1-2% of points sit just outside the hexagon drawn for their cell (22 of 2000 real shots at radius 10). That is faithful to d3-hexbin, sdvplot-js and sdvplot.

  • Squares are centered on (i * side, j * side) and half-open: a point exactly on an edge goes to the higher cell (JavaScript's Math.round(), which d3-hexbin uses). Every point lies inside its square.

Cells come in first-seen order: the cell of the first point first. Points with a missing or non-finite coordinate are skipped (sdvplot-js skips NaN; it would put an infinite one in a cell of its own).

Ids are strings, as in sdvplot-js's linked interactivity: a cell's id is "x,y", its center written as JavaScript writes a number (the shortest decimal that reads back exactly, -0 as 0), the data-sdv-id sdvplot-js stamps on the cell. The rim cell of a shot chart in the NBA legacy frame is "0,0" for either shape.

See also

geom_sdv_bins() to draw the cells, geom_sdv_bins_interactive() to link them to their points.

Examples

# three Brooklyn shots of 2025-26, NBA legacy frame (tenths of a foot,
# hoop at the origin): the two at the rim share a 1 ft hexagon
x <- c(0, -1, -44)
y <- c(0, 7, 252)
sdv_bins(x, y, radius = 10)
#>                   cell_id         x   y count weight rows
#> 1                     0,0   0.00000   0     2      2 1, 2
#> 2 -43.301270189221924,255 -43.30127 255     1      1    3
sdv_bins(x, y, shape = "square", side = 10)
#>   cell_id   x   y count weight rows
#> 1     0,0   0   0     1      1    1
#> 2    0,10   0  10     1      1    2
#> 3 -40,250 -40 250     1      1    3
sdv_bins(x, y, shape = "square", radius = 10, equal_area = TRUE)
#>                                  cell_id         x        y count weight rows
#> 1                                    0,0   0.00000   0.0000     2      2 1, 2
#> 2 -48.355646932059386,257.89678363765006 -48.35565 257.8968     1      1    3
sdv_bin_ids(x, y, radius = 10)
#> [1] "0,0"                     "0,0"                    
#> [3] "-43.301270189221924,255"
# the same shots in feet from the baseline, the hoop at (0, 5.25): a
# hoop-centered lattice puts them in the same cells, weighted by points
sdv_bins(x / 10, y / 10 + 5.25, radius = 1, origin = c(0, 5.25), weights = c(2, 2, 3))
#>                    cell_id         x     y count weight rows
#> 1                   0,5.25  0.000000  5.25     2      4 1, 2
#> 2 -4.330127018922193,30.75 -4.330127 30.75     1      3    3
